name: Piaui
summary_text: Piauí stands under Brazil's national framework for LGBTI people, and the source inventory records no state-level deviation from it. A trans visitor's status, documents and family recognition are therefore handled under the same rules that operate everywhere in the country, and Piauí's own courts have engaged with that machinery: a 2021 record documents a gender-recognition judgment issued through the state's judiciary.  Legal gender change requires no surgery, hormones or medical diagnosis, under the Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling of 1 March 2018, and proceeds by self-determination. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Council of Justice resolution of 14 May 2013, carried 14-1, with joint adoption available since 2010 and full adoption rights since 2015. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so entry and family matters are assessed on the same footing as for anyone else.  On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity to be a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. Courts have applied the prohibition to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita.  No third-gender option exists on identity documents nationwide, but civil-registry entries recording 'non-binary/unspecified' have been possible since 2020, and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 permits neutral-gender registry rectification and treats it as precedent. Documents therefore do not yet carry a non-binary marker in the ordinary case, and a visitor whose papers show a marker inconsistent with presentation should expect inspection at entry.  Detention carries a specific regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. Recognition as LGBTI for these purposes rests on self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.  Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women held in Rio de Janeiro state prisons between April and June 2021 interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region. It documents that such inmates are housed in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units, and treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights.  The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. OutRight International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions, and that the country retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife. In the October 2024 municipal elections, close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation.  Protection machinery has widened in parallel. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes.

name: Rio Grande do Sul
summary_text: Rio Grande do Sul stands under Brazil's national legal framework for LGBTI people. The sources covering this state record no deviation from that framework material enough to distinguish it, so a trans visitor in Rio Grande do Sul is governed by the same rules that apply in every other Brazilian state.  Same-sex marriage has been available nationwide since May 2013 under National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, which binds all civil registries and was adopted in a 14-1 vote. Spousal-visa equality and joint adoption follow from the same regime, with adoption rights in place since 2015. An expat legal guide updated on 5 April 2026 confirms that name and gender-marker changes require no surgery, so a visitor's documents are assessed on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.  On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court ruled in ADO 26 that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is a crime equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. Explicit national discrimination protections on those grounds have been in force since 2019, and courts have applied them to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing.  The text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. The same overview reports that no specific federal anti-discrimination statute exists, that repeal efforts are before Congress, and that intersex people lack specific protections.  Conditions vary with the size of place. Larger cities have legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas carry more social friction. Rio Grande do Sul has a substantial rural interior beyond the capital region, where that friction falls thickest and formal support is thinnest.  Arrest and imprisonment carry a defined regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are detained are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units, ask trans, travesti and intersex people which they prefer, and record the declared preference. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.
